title: Where do consultants go after consulting?
description: The common paths after consulting, from corporate strategy and private equity to start-ups, the public sector and staying to make partner.
hook: Many people join consulting knowing they will not stay forever, and that is completely normal. The skills you build travel well. Here are the paths people most commonly take afterwards.
body:
Common paths

  • Corporate strategy and business development inside large companies, often working on the same kinds of questions from the client side.
  • General management and operations roles, moving from advising to running a business unit.
  • Private equity and investing, especially for those who did due diligence and deals work.
  • Start-ups and scale-ups, in roles like strategy, operations or chief of staff, or founding their own company.
  • Public sector, policy and non-profits, using problem-solving skills for social impact.
  • Staying and working towards principal and partner.

Why consultants are in demand

Structured problem solving, comfort with data, clear communication and experience across industries are useful almost everywhere.

A healthy way to think about it

It is fine to be open about consulting being one step in a longer journey, but in interviews, focus on why you want to do the consulting job itself. Interviewers want people who are excited about the work, not just the exit.

Sources

  • Hacking the Case Interview: Consulting career path, levels and exits

Checked November 2026.

Choose the next skill, not just the next title

Consulting can lead into corporate strategy, business operations, product roles, entrepreneurship, investing, public service or specialist advisory work. These paths use different parts of the toolkit. A corporate strategy role may prioritise market analysis and executive communication; an operator needs ownership of recurring metrics; an investor may need deal judgement; a founder needs customer discovery and execution under uncertainty.

Imagine two consultants who both worked on a retailer's growth strategy. One built market-entry models and wants to join an internal strategy team. The other led a store pilot and wants to run a regional business. Their experience overlaps, but the evidence they should emphasise differs. The first should show how their analysis changed a strategic decision. The second should show how they navigated constraints and delivered measurable results.

When weighing an exit, ask how much decision ownership, people management, analytical depth and implementation exposure you will gain. A title or higher salary alone does not tell you whether the move builds the capabilities you care about. Look at the actual scope of the role and who will mentor you.
